edits.after: "feedback": "The lower own price and lower income can push quantity in opposite directions. An unchanged observed quantity may therefore conceal a positive own-price response offset by an inward demand shift; it does not identify elasticity on a fixed demand curve.",

edits.before: "q": "The Sovereign's final trial \u2014 A price decrease for X produces a positive substitution effect of +4 units and a negative income effect of -1 unit. What is the total change in quantity demanded?",
edits.after: "q": "After the price of X falls, the compensated move adds 4 units of X and the income effect removes 1 unit. An analyst claims that any negative income effect must make quantity fall after a price cut. What net quantity change contradicts that claim?",

edits.before:
"+3 units",
        "+5 units",
        "-3 units",
        "-5 units"
edits.after:
"An increase of 3 units",
        "An increase of 5 units",
        "A decrease of 3 units",
        "A decrease of 5 units"

edits.before: "feedback": "Total effect = substitution effect + income effect = 4 + (-1) = 3 units.",
edits.after: "feedback": "Adding the two effects gives +4-1=+3. The negative income effect identifies inferiority, but it is too small to overturn substitution, so X is not Giffen over this change.",

edits.before: "q": "The Sovereign's final trial \u2014 For a Giffen good, a rise in price makes the consumer effectively poorer. Why can that increase purchases of the good?",
edits.after: "q": "After a staple's price rises, a household is worse off but buys more of the staple. Preferences, money income, and other prices remain unchanged. Compensating the household back to its original utility at the new prices would instead make it buy less of the staple. What explains the difference between the compensated and actual choices?",

edits.before: "feedback": "The strong inferior-good income effect can dominate the ordinary substitution response.",
edits.after: "feedback": "The compensated comparison isolates substitution away from the more expensive staple. The actual price rise also lowers purchasing power. For this strongly inferior good, that income effect increases purchases by more than substitution reduces them, producing Giffen behavior.",

edits.before: "q": "The Sovereign's final trial \u2014 A researcher estimates a demand curve but omits a major preference trend correlated with price. What problem threatens the interpretation of the estimated price-quantity relationship?",
edits.after: "q": "A researcher observes higher prices and larger sales during a growing preference for a product. The trend is correlated with price but omitted from the analysis; income and related-good prices are controlled. Why can the positive fitted price coefficient fail to describe an upward-sloping demand curve?",

edits.before: "feedback": "If demand shifters move with price, the data do not isolate a single demand curve.",
edits.after: "feedback": "Controlling some demand determinants does not hold the omitted preference trend fixed. Its outward demand shifts can accompany higher observed prices and sales. The fitted coefficient can therefore mix shifts with movement along any one demand curve.",

edits.before: "q": "The Sovereign's final trial \u2014 Why does the area under a demand curve and above the market price represent consumer surplus?",
edits.after: "q": "A buyer values successive units at $12, $9, and $5, pays a uniform price of $6, and buys only units worth at least their price. An analyst counts both the buyer's payment and the value of the unpurchased third unit as consumer surplus. Which principle correctly separates surplus from those amounts?",

edits.before: "feedback": "Aggregating willingness-to-pay minus price across purchased units gives the area under demand above price.",
edits.after: "feedback": "Only the first two units are bought. Their surplus is (12-6)+(9-6)=$9. The $12 payment is expenditure, and the third unit creates no realized surplus because its value is below price. Summing willingness to pay minus price over purchased units gives consumer surplus.",

edits.before: "q": "The Sovereign's final trial \u2014 Why can market demand have a kink even when each individual's demand is smooth over the quantities they purchase?",
edits.after: "q": "Two buyers have individual demands Q₁=max(12-P,0) and Q₂=max(8-P,0). Each demand is smooth wherever its quantity is positive, yet the market curve changes slope at P=8. Why can horizontal aggregation create this kink without any change in either buyer's preferences?",

edits.before: "feedback": "As price changes, the set of consumers with positive demand can change, altering the slope of the aggregate demand curve.",
edits.after: "feedback": "Above P=8 only buyer 1 purchases, so market demand has dQ/dP=-1. Below P=8 both purchase, so the derivatives add to -2. The active set of buyers changes at the threshold, even though each positive-quantity segment is smooth.",

edits.before: "q": "The Sovereign's final trial \u2014 A firm's demand elasticity estimate changes along a linear demand curve even though the slope is constant. Why?",
edits.after: "q": "Demand is Q=100-2P. At P=$40 and P=$10, the slope dQ/dP is the same, yet a small price increase lowers revenue at the first point and raises it at the second. What reconciles these responses?",

edits.before: "feedback": "Point elasticity equals slope-related responsiveness multiplied by P/Q, so it varies along a linear curve.",
edits.after: "feedback": "At P=40, Q=20 and absolute point elasticity is 2×40/20=4. At P=10, Q=80 and it is 2×10/80=0.25. The common slope does not imply common elasticity because P/Q differs. Revenue responds differently in the elastic and inelastic regions.",

"imageAlt": "Two budget lines sharing a Y intercept, curves U0 and U1, and labeled bundles A, B and C.",
    "graphDescription": "Good X is horizontal and Good Y vertical, each from 0 to 50 in steps of 5, with no further units named. Blue Budget0 joins (0, 40) to (20, 0); green Budget1 joins (0, 40) to (40, 0), sharing the vertical intercept and extending farther right. In X-Y order, A is (10, 20), B is (20, 10), and C is (15, 25), with dashed guides to the axes. Purple U0 slopes downward through A and B, while dark-green U1 lies above it and touches Budget1 at C. Budget0 touches U0 at A. An unlabeled dashed orange line joins (0, 30) to (30, 0), runs parallel to Budget1, passes through A and touches U0 at B. No arrows or named effect labels are drawn."
edits.after:
"imageAlt": "Convex indifference curves with original optimum A (10,20), compensated optimum B (20,5), and final optimum C (15,25).",
    "graphDescription": "Good X is horizontal and Good Y vertical, each from 0 to 50. Original blue Budget 0 is 2X+Y=40, tangent to purple U0 at A=(10,20). Green Budget 1 is X+Y=40, tangent to dark green U1 at C=(15,25). The orange dashed compensated budget is X+Y=25, parallel to Budget 1 and tangent to U0 at B=(20,5); it supports U0 rather than crossing it. Both indifference curves are decreasing and strictly convex, and U1 lies above U0. The price of X falls from 2 to 1 with income 40 and Py=1. Substitution A to B raises X by 10 and lowers Y by 15. Income B to C lowers X by 5 and raises Y by 20, showing inferior X. Total A to C raises both X and Y by 5. Dotted guides mark all three coordinate pairs."
